title: Design Bounded Blocking Queue
statement:
On LeetCode this is a multithreading problem. Here each thread is an asynchronous task, and you coordinate the tasks with promises.

Design `BoundedBlockingQueue`, a first-in, first-out queue of integers that holds at most `capacity` elements and is shared by several threads:

- `new BoundedBlockingQueue(capacity)` creates an empty queue with that capacity.
- `enqueue(element)` adds `element` at the back. If the queue is full, the call waits until a slot frees up, and only then adds it.
- `dequeue()` removes and returns the element at the front. If the queue is empty, the call waits until an element is there to take.
- `size()` returns how many elements the queue holds right now.

When several calls are waiting at once, release them in the order they started waiting. Make `enqueue` and `dequeue` `async` and wait on promises rather than timers, so that a waiting call returns at the very moment it can.

Each case gives `producers`, `consumers`, `operations` and `args`. `operations[0]` is `"BoundedBlockingQueue"` with `args[0] = [capacity]`; every later entry is `"enqueue"` with `args[i] = [element]` or `"dequeue"` with `args[i] = []`. Producer threads make the enqueue calls and consumer threads the dequeue calls, dealt out in turn: the first enqueue goes to producer 1, the next to producer 2 and so on, starting over after the last producer, and the same for dequeues and consumers. The call at index `i` is made at `i` ms, or, if its thread is still waiting in its previous call at that moment, as soon as that call returns. When every call has returned, `size()` is called once.

The answer is `{ output, times }`. `output` is LeetCode's output: the value returned by each dequeue call, in the order of `operations`, followed by the final size. `times[i - 1]` is the time in ms at which the call at index `i` returned.
constraints: There are 1 to 40 calls to enqueue and dequeue in total
dequeue calls <= enqueue calls <= dequeue calls + capacity, so every call eventually returns
signature: Object BoundedBlockingQueue(int producers, int consumers, String[] operations, int[][] args)
api: class BoundedBlockingQueue { constructor(capacity: number); enqueue(element: number): void | Promise<void>; dequeue(): number | Promise<number>; size(): number }
notes:
## Intuition

A blocking queue is an ordinary queue plus two reasons to wait: a producer waits while the queue is full, a consumer while it is empty. Each reason gets its own line of parked callers. A caller that must wait creates a promise, parks its `resolve` function in the matching line and awaits it. Whoever changes the condition wakes the first caller in the other line: an enqueue makes the queue non-empty, so it wakes one consumer; a dequeue frees a slot, so it wakes one producer. A woken caller checks its condition again in a `while` loop before acting. (The brute force instead keeps every call as a request and, after each change, grants the oldest requests that can go ahead.)

## Approach

1. Keep `items` (the elements, front first), `capacity`, and two lines of resolve functions: `waitingProducers` and `waitingConsumers`.
2. `enqueue(element)`: while `items` is full, park in `waitingProducers` and await. Then push `element` and wake the first waiting consumer, if any.
3. `dequeue()`: while `items` is empty, park in `waitingConsumers` and await. Then shift the front `element`, wake the first waiting producer, if any, and return `element`.
4. `size()` returns `items.length`.

With real threads this is a lock with two condition variables, `notFull` and `notEmpty`: `enqueue` locks, waits on `notFull` while full, adds, signals `notEmpty` and unlocks; `dequeue` mirrors it. Another classic design uses two counting semaphores, `slots` starting at `capacity` and `filled` starting at 0, plus a mutex around the queue itself. JavaScript runs one task at a time, so the code between two `await`s already acts as the locked region; parking a resolve function plays the part of waiting, and calling it the part of signalling.

## Example 1, step by step

Capacity 2, one producer and one consumer; call `i` is made at `i` ms.

- 1 ms: `enqueue(1)` adds 1. 2 ms: `dequeue()` returns 1.
- 3 ms: `dequeue()` finds `items` empty and parks in `waitingConsumers`.
- 4 ms: `enqueue(0)` adds 0 and wakes the consumer, which takes 0: both calls return at 4 ms.
- 5 and 6 ms: 2 and 3 are added, so `items = [2, 3]` is full.
- 7 ms: `enqueue(4)` parks in `waitingProducers`.
- 8 ms: `dequeue()` takes 2 and wakes the producer, which adds 4; both return at 8 ms.
- `size()` is 2, so the answer is `{ output: [1, 0, 2, 2], times: [1, 2, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8, 8] }`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(capacity) per call for `items.shift()` (O(1) with a ring buffer or index pointer), plus O(1) to park or wake.
- Space: O(capacity + w) for the elements and the w callers waiting at once.

## Pitfalls

- Checking with `if` instead of `while`: a woken caller must look again before it acts, as condition variables also require.
- Forgetting to wake the other side: a parked consumer sleeps forever if `enqueue` does not resolve it.
- Waking callers out of order (`pop` instead of `shift`) breaks the first-come, first-served rule.
- Polling with `setTimeout` returns late and never lets virtual time move on; wait on promises.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `capacity` | the most elements the queue may hold |
| `items` | the elements in the queue, front first |
| `waitingProducers` | resolve functions of enqueue calls waiting for a free slot, oldest first |
| `waitingConsumers` | resolve functions of dequeue calls waiting for an element, oldest first |
| `wake` | the resolve function of the caller being released, if any |
| `element` | the value being added or removed |

narration.10: A producer may only add when there is room; the loop re-checks after every wake-up.
narration.11: Park: the promise resolves when a dequeue frees a slot and calls this resolve function.

narration.15: Resolving its promise lets that dequeue continue.

narration.20: Park until an enqueue brings an element and wakes this consumer.
narration.22: Take the element at the front.
narration.23: A slot is free now: pick the producer that has waited longest.
narration.24: Wake it so its enqueue can finish.
narration.25: Return the element that was taken.
